section_summary: This section combines translated Japanese and Chinese press material, Allied and Soviet diplomatic reporting, and captured-document analysis concerning Japan’s wartime government, political organizations, economy, industrial dispersal, public morale, and prospects for defeat. It also contains administrative cross-references and correspondence about biographical intelligence on Japanese figures, including requests for translations of Japanese Who’s Who volumes. The final pages include a private inquiry about Baron Tanetarō Megata and the opening of an embassy report based on testimony from a Chinese student recently returned from Japan.

subfiles.title: Cabinet advisers and the Composite Planning Board
subfiles.about: Continuation of an analysis of the Koiso cabinet’s expanded advisory system and its new Composite Planning Board.
subfiles.summary: The article explains that cabinet advisers were no longer confined to wartime economic questions but were selected from diplomatic, military, educational, agricultural, political, and industrial circles. It identifies Arita and Suematsu as especially influential political advisers and describes the informal way in which Koiso consulted the group. The second part outlines the Composite Planning Board’s coordinating, investigative, and experimental functions and lists Haniba and its departmental directors.

subfiles.title: New Governor: appointment of Kyuichirō Totsuka
subfiles.about: Reports Totsuka’s appointment as governor of Fukuoka and to several concurrent wartime administrative posts.
subfiles.summary: The clipping announces that Kyuichirō Totsuka became governor of Fukuoka, head of the Kyushu mines district, head of the Moji oceanic-communications bureau, and local military-supply supervisor. It notes his age, education at Tokyo Imperial University, former governorship of Hokkaido, and service in Yamaguchi, Miyagi, and Tokushima.

subfiles.title: The Budget of the “Mongolian Government”
subfiles.about: Summarizes the sharply enlarged 1945 budget of the Japanese-sponsored Mongolian government.
subfiles.summary: The Political Congress approved expenditures of 276,750,000 yuan, nearly twice the preceding year’s total, with the prosecution of the war identified as the principal priority. The blurred remainder mentions increased tax income and a planned issue of 180,000,000 yuan in highway bonds.

subfiles.title: Japanese New Fascist Party in the Formative Stage
subfiles.to: American Embassy, Chongqing and U.S. agencies
subfiles.about: Analyzes efforts to dissolve the Assistance Political Association and create a broader Japanese wartime political party.
subfiles.summary: The report traces party-reorganization proposals from the Tōjō period through the Koiso cabinet and the Diet’s current session. It describes the proposed dissolution of the Assistance Political Association, Koiso’s support, and plans to turn the Imperial Rule Assistance Association and its youth brigade into government auxiliaries. The editors interpret the projected party as a fascist device for mobilizing and deceiving a wider segment of the population.

subfiles.title: Advocacy of Japanese Diet Members for the “New Party”
subfiles.to: American Embassy, Chongqing and U.S. agencies
subfiles.about: Presents statements by three Diet members and a magazine editorial supporting a reorganized Japanese political party.
subfiles.summary: Nakajima, Matsumura, and Kigurashi criticize the lack of popular roots, unity, and local organization in the existing wartime associations. Matsumura argues that permitting organization would expose antiwar elements, while Kigurashi calls for a stronger national political organization. An Oriental Economics editorial condemns both assistance associations as failures and supports forming one or more new parties.

subfiles.title: The Urgent Installation of Underground Factories for Protection Against Air Raids
subfiles.doc_type: translated technical press article with inserted control sheets
subfiles.to: Co-ordinated Translation Center and U.S. agencies
subfiles.about: Advocates moving Japanese war production underground and discusses suitable geology, layouts, equipment, costs, and industries.
subfiles.summary: The article argues that dispersal alone cannot protect industry from air attack and cites German, Soviet, Maginot Line, and Rabaul examples to support underground factories and cities. It describes strategic benefits, geological and groundwater requirements, tunnel dimensions, blast protection, drainage, ventilation, lighting, gas defense, and material costs. It recommends government-assisted syndicates for tunnel construction and prioritizes aircraft-engine, communications, radar, precision-instrument, and some chemical production; pages 122–123 are largely illegible State Department processing sheets inserted before the translation resumes.

subfiles.title: New Japanese Economic Policy in China Will Be Realized Soon
subfiles.from: Shansi Hwa Pei Hsin Pao, Taiyuan
subfiles.to: American Embassy, Chongqing and U.S. agencies
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese plans for centralized control of Chinese resources, prices, purchasing, distribution, and transport.
subfiles.summary: Shigemitsu tells the Diet that Japan intends to strengthen its control over Chinese resources and inflation through a new supreme economic council. The council would combine delegates from Japanese organizations in China and work with the Shanghai Japanese Economic Council’s price committee. Implementation was expected after Minister Horiuchi returned to China.

subfiles.title: Telegram 3732: British assessment of the Suzuki cabinet
subfiles.from: John G. Winant, American Embassy, London
subfiles.about: Summarizes a British interdepartmental assessment of the fall of the Koiso cabinet and the political composition of Suzuki’s government.
subfiles.summary: The British assessment doubts that Soviet denunciation of the neutrality pact directly caused Koiso’s fall, although anticipation of it may have mattered. Suzuki is portrayed as a respected figure heading a carefully balanced cabinet that could be presented as nationalist, conciliatory, or professionally competent as circumstances required. The telegram concludes that the cabinet is likely to continue the war and offers to send further summaries from London’s Far Eastern propaganda meetings.

subfiles.title: Reply requesting continued London summaries
subfiles.from: Edward R. Stettinius Jr., Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Requests continued telegraphic summaries of useful British analysis of Far Eastern affairs.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that London’s summary of combined British thinking was interesting and useful. It asks the embassy to continue transmitting similar summaries whenever they would assist the Department.

subfiles.title: Despatch 1618 transmitting Zhukov’s analysis of Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits a translation of E. Zhukov’s Red Star article on Japan’s internal political situation.
subfiles.summary: The embassy characterizes Zhukov as the foremost Soviet press author on Japan and describes the article as comprehensive and dispassionate. It highlights his discussion of psychological changes, food and production problems, imported Korean and Chinese labor, and the declining popularity of the war. Copies were also directed to Chongqing and the U.S. political advisers in the China Theater.

subfiles.title: The Internal Political Situation of Japan
subfiles.to: American Embassy, Moscow and Department of State
subfiles.about: Surveys Japanese political institutions, wartime organizations, economic strain, manpower problems, and deteriorating public morale.
subfiles.summary: Zhukov traces the decline of parliamentary politics, the failures of the Association and Political Association for Aid to the Throne, and the limited revival of former party politicians after Tōjō’s fall. He describes conflict over the Youth Union and argues that the Koiso–Yonai cabinet remained trapped between parliamentary and reactionary forces. Military reverses, bombing, industrial underproduction, food scarcity, manpower mobilization, and reliance on colonial labor are presented as evidence that the war had become unpopular and that official defensive rhetoric was losing credibility.

subfiles.title: Telegram 1172: Pravda on Japan’s military-political difficulties
subfiles.from: W. Averell Harriman, American Embassy, Moscow
subfiles.about: Summarizes A. Semonov’s Pravda article on Japan’s cabinet crisis, military reverses, and political reorganization.
subfiles.summary: Semonov links Japan’s governmental change to approaching invasion, intensified bombing, economic weakness, and the failure of the Koiso cabinet to solve problems inherited from Tōjō. He interprets the proposed new party and dissolution of the assistance associations as maneuvers to simulate abandonment of fascism and distract the population from defeat. Germany’s imminent collapse is said to worsen Japan’s increasingly desperate position.

subfiles.title: Telegram 1227: “Worsening of Japan’s Military and Political Situation”
subfiles.from: George F. Kennan, American Embassy, Moscow
subfiles.about: Reports a Soviet journal article assessing Japan’s military reverses, economic crisis, and proposed political-party changes.
subfiles.summary: Arkadyev argues that Koiso failed to improve military performance, production, food supply, or morale while American victories and bombing placed Japan under mounting pressure. The proposed party is interpreted as the first step in discarding a Nazi-style political structure and creating the appearance of renewed constitutional parliamentary government. Kennan notes that the article’s emphasis on Germany’s collapse might support a future Soviet claim to major credit for the Pacific outcome.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Sir Robert Craigie on the Suzuki government
subfiles.about: Points to an article by Sir Robert Craigie on the significance of the Suzuki government’s accession to power.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records that the original article was transmitted from London under another file classification. It supplies the relevant date and reference number but contains none of Craigie’s argument.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Indian nationalist reaction to abandonment of the “Greater Asia” policy
subfiles.about: Refers to press clippings on Indian nationalist responses to Japan’s abandonment of its “Greater Asia” policy.
subfiles.summary: The note directs researchers to the original Bombay document filed under a different decimal number. It identifies the subject and date but does not reproduce the clippings.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting a Japanese Document Report
subfiles.from: Robert Murphy, United States Political Adviser for Germany
subfiles.about: Transmits a SHAEF Japanese Document Report concerning conditions in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Murphy encloses the report issued by the office of SHAEF’s assistant chief of staff, G-2, on April 11. The short letter serves solely as the covering communication for the captured German report that follows.

subfiles.title: Japanese Document Report: Conditions in Japan
subfiles.from: Office of the Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, SHAEF
subfiles.to: Allied military, naval, air, economic, and political intelligence recipients
subfiles.about: Reproduces a German engineer’s observations of Japanese society, politics, surveillance, industry, and wartime attitudes during 1941–1942.
subfiles.summary: The engineer describes rationing, taxation, mobilization, civil defense, obedience to state authority, reverence for the emperor, and acceptance of wartime sacrifice, while acknowledging that the war itself was not popular. He discusses Japanese attitudes toward Germans and other foreigners, police surveillance, racial and cultural distance, and Japan’s pursuit of dominance in East Asia. The report also emphasizes industrial secrecy, synthetic-fuel work, exploitation of foreign technology, and the need for Germany to restrict Japanese access to sensitive facilities.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: proposed return of Sava Kirov to Bulgaria
subfiles.about: Refers to a report that the Sofia Foreign Office asked Sava Kirov to return to Bulgaria.
subfiles.summary: The sheet states that Allied Control Commission consent for Kirov’s return had allegedly been granted. It directs the reader to the original Bern telegram under the Bulgaria control file.

subfiles.title: Request for translation of a Japanese International Who’s Who
subfiles.from: Frederick B. Lyon, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation
subfiles.to: Lt. Col. Edward H. Miller, Military Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: Requests War Department exploration of translating politically useful portions of a Japanese biographical reference work.
subfiles.summary: Lyon forwards a pictorial Japanese International Who’s Who believed to contain extensive information on left-wing and liberal Japanese figures concealed among broader celebrity biographies. He argues that selected translations could assist U.S. operations in Japan and requests copies for both the State and War Departments. Distribution outside State, War, and Navy was to require State Department clearance, while entries on athletes and actors could be omitted.

subfiles.title: Internal memorandum on the Japanese Who’s Who
subfiles.about: Asks that a Japanese biographical volume supplied by Eugene Dooman be presented to the appropriate War Department section for translation.
subfiles.summary: Van Oss repeats Dooman’s assessment that the volume concentrates on Japanese left-wing individuals while using other prominent biographies as a cloak. He requests high security, a specified number of translated copies for State, and prior clearance through Dooman for distribution outside State and War. Non-Japanese and nonpolitical entries were considered unnecessary.

subfiles.title: Routing note concerning the Japanese Who’s Who
subfiles.about: Briefly routes the Japanese Who’s Who material for further handling.
subfiles.summary: Most of the handwritten text is illegible in the OCR. The surviving wording appears to direct Longyear to pass or present the material to Colonel Miller.

subfiles.title: Return of the Japanese Who’s Who
subfiles.about: Returns the Japanese Who’s Who and identifies a newer Federal Communications Commission report on Japanese personalities.
subfiles.summary: Longyear returns the volume, noting the War Department’s low opinion of it. He instead points Dooman to the Federal Broadcast Intelligence Service’s Radio Report on the Far East No. 70, a special Who’s Who in Japan dated May 25, 1945, and provides contact information for obtaining copies. The exact day in the damaged June date is unclear.

subfiles.title: Request for Who’s Who in Japan and Japanese Occupied Territories
subfiles.about: Requests three copies of a British intelligence Who’s Who for State Department research on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Lyon asks whether the fourth edition of Part A, Japan, prepared by the British Ministry of Information in New Delhi, can be supplied to State. Copies were wanted for the Commodities Division’s Japanese industry studies and for two other State divisions. He also requests later parts of the work if available.

subfiles.title: War Department reply on the requested Who’s Who
subfiles.from: Lt. Col. Edward H. Miller, War Department
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports that the requested British Who’s Who was unavailable in Washington and recommends obtaining it from New Delhi.
subfiles.summary: Miller states that neither the War Department nor the British Military Mission possessed the document in Washington. Since it apparently had only field distribution, he recommends requesting it through the American diplomatic mission in New Delhi from the local joint intelligence agency.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about Baron Tanetarō Megata
subfiles.about: Asks whether Baron Tanetarō Megata, whose 1921 London photograph Lull had acquired, was active in the current war.
subfiles.summary: Lull explains that he obtained a large cabinet photograph labeled with variants of Megata’s name while purchasing an autograph collection. Judging from the portrait, he describes Megata as a kindly businessman and requests any available biographical information. A return stamp was enclosed.

subfiles.title: State Department reply concerning Tanetarō Megata
subfiles.from: Erle R. Dickover, Division of Japanese Affairs
subfiles.about: Identifies the photographed man as Baron Tanetarō Megata and reports that he died in 1926.
subfiles.summary: Dickover cites a New York Times notice of Megata’s death on September 10, 1926, and encloses a transcription from a 1919 biographical source. He warns that gaps in the Department’s reference collection prevent coverage of Megata’s final years and disclaims responsibility for the outside source’s accuracy. Lull’s stamp is returned.

subfiles.title: Biographical data on Baron Tanetarō Megata
subfiles.from: Transcription from a 1919 Who’s Who in Japan
subfiles.about: Provides a short career sketch of Japanese financial administrator Baron Tanetarō Megata.
subfiles.summary: The damaged transcription records Megata’s birth, family, Harvard education, and successive posts in Japanese financial and revenue administration. It notes service as financial adviser to the Korean government, elevation to the peerage for work connected with the Russo-Japanese War, and a 1917 mission to the United States as commissioner of finance and economy. His address is given in Koishikawa, Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of a Chinese student’s account of conditions in Japan
subfiles.from: Edward E. Rice, American Embassy, Chongqing
subfiles.to: Major General Patrick J. Hurley, American ambassador
subfiles.about: Transmits testimony from a Chinese industrial-engineering student who left Japan in October 1944.
subfiles.summary: Rice introduces an enclosed memorandum based on a young Chinese student’s three years of study in Japan and on later reports from fellow students encountered in North China. The informant describes subsistence below healthy minimums, the mobilization of secondary and college students, and severe shortages of coal, oil, and other materials that were paralyzing the economy. The enclosure itself follows beyond this section.
